summary: The note examines herbal medicine's continuing role in modern healthcare, covering its ancient history, strong market demand, and the risks created by weak regulation and poor quality control. It contrasts the EU's registration-based approach with the looser US supplement regime and describes consumer-education efforts like the Herb Identity Project. It concludes that herbal medicine can contribute to healthcare if guided by safety, efficacy, research, standardization and responsible use.
one_line: Herbal medicine remains widely used and commercially strong, but uneven regulation and quality control raise safety concerns that need standards, research and consumer education.
key_facts: Herbal medicine has documented use dating back thousands of years, including in ancient Egypt, China, and Greece.
In September 2023 the World Health Organization (WHO) reported that approximately 80% of the world's population still uses some form of herbal medicine.
A Global Wellness Institute report published October 5, 2023 projected the herbal supplement market to reach $8 billion by the end of the year.

Dr. Jacob Feinstein, a pharmacologist and regulatory consultant, warns herbal medicines contain active compounds that can interact with other medications, cause side effects, or be toxic, and that variable concentration of active ingredients is a major safety concern.
Unlike pharmaceuticals, herbs marketed as dietary supplements avoid the comprehensive scrutiny and FDA approval required of drugs.
Quality control problems in the herbal industry include plant misidentification, contamination with other herbs, pesticides or heavy metals, and adulteration with synthetic drugs.
On November 2, 2023, authorities in a raid seized thousands of bottles of adulterated supplements from a New York warehouse; labeled 'pure' herbal extracts, they contained undeclared pharmaceuticals.
The European Union's Traditional Herbal Medicinal Products Directive requires herbal products to be registered and undergo safety and efficacy assessments.
In the United States, the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 significantly limits the FDA's authority to regulate supplements.
The National Herbal Alliance launched the 'Herb Identity Project' starting December 2023, with universities and research entities, to build a public database of verified herbal products.
Dr. Linda O'Neil, an ethnobotanist at the University of Natural Health, says herbal medicine is a holistic approach addressing root causes of disease.
Many in healthcare are calling for more research, better standardization practices, and a global regulatory framework for herbal medicine.
